result:
The final answer is in `final.py`. Its search score is **0.5913**, against 0.365 for the LRU baseline, and I used **19 of the 24 scorer calls**. I couldn't score it on the hidden split. The only out-of-sample check I could run was a set of seeds in my own trace generator that I never tuned on.

| | Search score (official) | My held-out seeds |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline (LRU) | 0.365 | — |
| First champion (LIRS) | 0.566 | 0.572 |
| Final pick (`final.py`) | **0.5913** | 0.522* |

\*Not comparable with the LIRS figure: I added two harder trace types (drift and hot-with-scans) after measuring LIRS, which lowers everyone's numbers. On the same seeds, the best single policy scored 0.517 and the earlier ensemble 0.594 → 0.522 range collapsed accordingly.

**Why it beats LRU.** The core is a policy that predicts when each key will next be requested. It evicts the key expected furthest in the future, which approximates the optimal policy that knows the future.
- **Predicted next use:** the last access plus the key's average gap between requests. Keys seen only a few times have their estimate pulled toward a cautious default, so one lucky repeat doesn't make a key look hot.
- **Overdue keys:** a key that is late for its next request is treated as aging, the way LRU would treat it.
- **Brand-new keys:** a new key's expected gap is learned from the traffic, as the average return distance divided by the share of new keys that ever come back. During scans that share is low, so one-off keys are cheap to drop.
- **Not caching a key at all:** if an incoming key is expected later than the best eviction candidate, it isn't stored. That keeps loops stable and protects hot keys from scans. How readily it does this adjusts itself: wrong decisions (the skipped key comes back first) make it more reluctant, right ones make it bolder.
- **Memory:** it remembers keys for up to 200× capacity after eviction.

An LRU shadow runs alongside. The cache only switches to LRU's contents when LRU has clearly been ahead for a while, by more than the cost of replacing that many keys. On the scorer's six traces it never switches, so the score is exactly the predictor's. On my traces where popularity drifts steadily, it recovers about +0.05 hit rate there, where the predictor alone trails LRU badly.

**Families tried first:**
| Approach | Official | My harness (at the time) |
|---|---|---|
| ARC | 0.407 | 0.442 |
| S3-FIFO | — | 0.444 |
| W-TinyLFU | 0.503 | 0.462 |
| LIRS | 0.566 | 0.469 |
| Adaptive-window TinyLFU, LIRS with admission filter, LIRS with self-tuning queue size | — | each no better than LIRS |

**Candidate log (official calls):**
| Candidate | Score | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| lirs / wtlfu / arc | 0.566 / 0.503 / 0.407 | Checked my harness ranks them the same as the scorer |
| Ensemble of LIRS, LRU and TinyLFU, following the recent leader | 0.5767 | Kept |
| Same, with switch hysteresis | 0.5796 | Kept |
| Ensemble with a switch-cost gate, plus a first prediction policy | 0.5786 / 0.5808 | Small gain |
| Prediction policy alone, with "don't cache" | 0.5854 | Kept; ensemble version 0.5847 |
| Remember evicted keys for 40× / 200× capacity | 0.5882 / 0.5887 | Kept |
| Ensemble with LRU, TinyLFU and LIRS | 0.5876 | Dropped |
| "Don't cache" threshold that adjusts itself | 0.5892 | Kept |
| Ensemble variants | 0.5865 / 0.5884 | Dropped (lose on phases) |
| Pull rarely seen keys toward the default | **0.5913** | Kept |
| Predictor + LRU shadow (= `final.py`, confirmed) | 0.5913 / 0.5913 | Final |

**What I learned along the way:**
- Ensembles helped until the prediction policy matured. After that, extra members just cost switching losses.
- Ghost history and pulling rarely seen keys toward the default were what moved the scorer's hard traces (hot_with_scans, mixed).
- My harness stopped telling candidates apart near the end. I added traces generated from the task description (hot keys with scans, drifting popularity) rather than from scorer data.
- I found and fixed one harness bug mid-run. Fast parameter sweeps were sometimes reusing stale compiled code. I re-ran the affected comparisons; the earlier ensemble sweeps were not affected.

The scorer's run takes about 1s, well under the 8s limit. `final.py` passes my per-step checks: never over capacity, hits counted correctly, and only the requested key ever added. The scorer accepted it. Working files and the harness are in `work/`.
